The ticking is the argument: thirty-seven days in which everyone had time to stop.
A chapter about a document, not a battle — machinery, not mood.
The siege guns. Never a victory march: the forts fall, and the point is the machinery.
Antwerp, Namur and Maubeuge — the same machinery, still grinding.
The encounter battles in the fog.
The counter-attack that bent the wheel, in the middle of the retreat.
The hinge holding while it is taken apart to feed the west.
Two corps that fought in neither battle they were sent to decide.
The only forward motion in the score.
The pre-campaign window the July Crisis and the ultimatum occupy.
Mobilization and Liège: the timetable turning into movement.
The Frontiers and the Great Retreat. One cue for three stages, because this stretch should feel like it will not end.

22 August 1914, the bloodiest day in French history: about 27,000 French dead. The music stops. A narrower window than the retreat around it, so it wins — silence after an hour of sound is the strongest thing the site can do, and the pack already refuses to gamify this day (ADR 0008).
The Aisne, the race to the sea, First Ypres and the line. The war becomes geography.
